title: That's Amaro!
summary: Josh and Chuck open with live show announcements (DC, Boston, Toronto in May) and a bit of banter about Josh's habit of making up songs and sipping amaro. The main topic is amaro, the Italian bitter herbal liqueur: what it is, how it is made, its bittering agents and botanicals, amari versus cocktail bitters and vermouth, and its history from Arab alchemists and Italian monasteries through the 19th-century commercial boom. They cover Campari and the Americano, the Negroni origin story, Averna, Montenegro, Chartreuse, Cynar, Fernet-Branca, and American amari. They discuss whether amaro aids digestion, then close with a listener email about fructose intolerance and honey and a reminder about honey for infants.

segments.title: Live show announcements and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh announces May live shows in Washington DC, Boston, and Toronto with ticket presale details, then talks about making up songs and sipping amaro.

segments.title: What amaro is and how it is made
segments.summary: Amaro is defined as a bitter, sweetened herbal liqueur, usually Italian, often used as a digestif or aperitif. Its base spirit, bittering agents, and proprietary botanical blends are described, along with the basic maceration and aging process.

segments.title: Bittering agents and the Italian taste for bitter
segments.summary: Gentian, wormwood, and cinchona are discussed as key bittering agents. The hosts discuss Italian fondness for bitter flavors and their own changing tastes for bitter foods and drinks.

segments.title: Amaro botanicals and sipping versus shots
segments.summary: Chuck reads a list of amaro botanicals, including artichoke, orange peel, caraway, chamomile, cloves, cinnamon, fennel, rhubarb, sarsaparilla, and yerba mate. They discuss amaro's lighter proof compared with spirits and how it is used in spritzers.

segments.title: Amaro versus cocktail bitters and vermouth
segments.summary: Cocktail bitters are higher proof and used in dashes, while amari are sipped. Vermouth is compared with amaro as an aromatized fortified wine, and the Massi Napa Valley sweet vermouth and Carpano Antica are mentioned.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break; Chuck mentions drinking lemon water spiked with moonshine.

segments.title: Early history: Arab alchemists, monasteries, and Pope Boniface VIII
segments.summary: Distillation and infusion are traced to Arab alchemists in the seventh and eighth centuries. Medicinal cocktails such as the julep and crème de violette-based drinks are mentioned. Italian monasteries made medicinal elixirs, and Pope Boniface VIII is said to have been treated for kidney stones with an herbal liqueur in 1300.

segments.title: Spread of amaro in the 1800s and classic brands
segments.summary: Spice trade and sugar from the New World shaped modern amaro. Apothecaries sold amari and the drink became recreational in the nineteenth century. Campari's origin, the carmine coloring, and the Americano and Negroni origin stories are described. Averna and Montenegro's origin stories are covered.

segments.title: Chartreuse, Cynar, Fernet-Branca, and American amari
segments.summary: Chartreuse is described as a monastery liqueur with 132 botanicals known to only two monks, and its green color is named after the liqueur. Cynar's artichoke branding and Fernet-Branca's popularity in Argentina, including the fernet and Coke drink, are discussed. American amari are mentioned briefly.

segments.title: Does amaro aid digestion?
segments.summary: The hosts examine whether amaro works as a digestif, citing the bitter taste response, herbal properties, and mixed evidence on alcohol slowing digestion. They conclude it is a pleasant way to end a meal, and that cocktail bitters before a meal may work better.

segments.title: Listener mail: honey, fructose intolerance, and infant botulism
segments.summary: A listener named Taylor Hadden writes that honey is a trigger for people with fructose intolerance and that dextrose can help. The hosts add a reminder that honey should not be fed to babies under one year old.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and provide the email address for contact.
